summary: A German verb changes its ending for every person: you take the stem (the infinitive without -en: koch-en, trink-en, kauf-en) and add -e, -st, -t for ich, du, er/sie/es and -en, -t, -en for wir, ihr, sie/Sie. Polite Sie always takes the plural form (Sie trinken). A group of strong verbs also changes the stem vowel, but only in the du and er/sie/es forms: essen → du isst, er isst (e → i); later you will meet a → ä (fahren → du fährst). The modal verbs wollen and mögen are irregular: no ending in ich and er (ich will, er will; ich mag, er mag) and another vowel in the singular. Their polite cousin möchte (would like) is a form of mögen used like a present: ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte, wir möchten. sein and haben are irregular too (ich bin, du bist, er ist …; du hast, er hat). German has one present tense for “I eat”, “I am eating” and often “I will eat” – there is no -ing form. The finite verb always stands in second place in a statement (Ich trinke Tee. Vielleicht trinke ich Tee.); with a modal, the second verb goes to the very end as an infinitive (Ich will Tee trinken).

blocks.title: Verb second
blocks.text: In a statement the conjugated verb is always the second element: Ich trinke Tee. – Natürlich trinke ich Tee. – Vielleicht kocht er. Whatever comes first (subject, adverb, object), the verb stays in place two and the subject moves behind it if needed.

blocks.caption: With a modal (wollen, mögen, möchte): the modal is second, the other verb waits at the end in the infinitive

blocks.title: No -ing form
blocks.text: Ich esse = I eat and I am eating. Never *Ich bin essen. The present also covers plans: Morgen koche ich (I’ll cook tomorrow).

blocks.title: du isst = er isst
blocks.text: A stem ending in s, ss, ß or z adds only -t for du: du isst (not *issst), du heißt. So du and er look the same: du isst, er isst.

blocks.title: Ich will is not “I will”
blocks.text: wollen means “to want”: Ich will Kaffee = I want coffee. In a shop or café möchte is more polite: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.

items.title: English
points: and a separate -ing form (I am eating) that German does not have

askYourself: Who is the subject? ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie or polite Sie (= the plural form)?
What is the stem? Drop -en from the infinitive (koch-en → koch-).
Is it a vowel-changing verb (essen) with du or er/sie/es? → isst.
Is it a modal (wollen, mögen)? → ich will / er will, ich mag / er mag – no ending; polite wish: möchte.
Is it sein or haben? → learn the forms by heart.
Is the verb in second place? Is a second verb at the end in the infinitive?
steps: Take the stem and add the ending (or the irregular form).
Put the verb in second place; a second verb goes to the end.

traps: du isst, er isst – the same form; not *du esst (esst is ihr).
ich will, er will, ich mag, er mag: modals have no -e and no -t.
Polite Sie takes the plural: Sie trinken, Sie möchten, Sie sind.
No progressive: Ich esse (I am eating), not *Ich bin essen.
Verb second: Vielleicht trinke ich Tee – not *Vielleicht ich trinke Tee.
With a modal the second verb is an infinitive at the end: Ich will Tee trinken – not *Ich will trinke Tee.

quiz.why: essen changes e → i for du and er/sie/es; after ss only -t: du isst.
No vowel change in the plural: ihr esst.
Modals have no ending in the er-form: er will.
Polite Sie takes the plural form.
Verb second: when the object comes first, the subject moves behind the verb.
The modal is second and conjugated; the other verb is an infinitive at the end.
er möchte – like ich möchte, no -t.

seeAlso.note: Arabic marks the person with prefixes and endings on the imperfect: آكُلُ ʾākulu (I eat), تَأْكُلُ taʾkulu (you eat, to a man), يَأْكُلُ yaʾkulu (he eats).
The Hebrew present changes for gender and number, not for person: אוֹכֵל / אוֹכֶלֶת / אוֹכְלִים / אוֹכְלוֹת – so the pronoun is always needed.
Chinese verbs never change: 我吃, 你吃, 他吃; time words and particles (在, 了) do the work German does with endings and context.
The verbs of this lesson take an object in the accusative: Ich trinke einen Kaffee.
